implementation_notes: The canonical Java form from the pattern's own example: a class per table with private fields per column, accessors, an update()/insert() that prepares a parameterised statement and a separate finder class (or static find methods) that runs the SELECT and calls a load(ResultSet) factory. This is manual support - JDBC gives statements and result sets, never the row object - but it is the shape most code-generation templates and legacy persistence layers produce, and it keeps SQL visible for review.
pitfalls: Connections and statements must be closed with try-with-resources; an unclosed PreparedStatement keeps the cursor and connection busy.
Without an Identity Map two finder calls return two objects for one row and the second update overwrites the first (lost update).
SQLException leaks the driver into callers; wrap it in a persistence-agnostic exception at the gateway boundary.

variants.name: jOOQ generated UpdatableRecord (store/refresh/delete)
variants.implementation_notes: jOOQ's code generator emits one Record class per table that is a real row object: it holds the column values, tracks dirty fields, and persists itself through store() (insert or update), refresh() and delete(), with the connection attached to the record's configuration. That is the closest the JVM ecosystem comes to a library-provided Row Data Gateway, but it is attached to a jOOQ Configuration and requires code generation plus the jOOQ runtime; hand-written JDBC remains the dependency-free option.
pitfalls: A record fetched from one Configuration is attached to that configuration's connection; using it after the connection is returned to the pool is unsafe.
store() decides insert vs update from the record's internal flag, so a record built by hand can insert where an update was intended - use update() when that matters.
